Let the judges here take heed how dangerous it is, and full of peril, singularly in criminal matters, where the honour and the life of a man are treated of, to found a judgment upon the deposition of witnesses: who oftentimes pertinaciously assure false things to be true <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, from which afterwards they are constrained to depart. Let the judges see also how much surer it is, even for a sovereign judgment, not to rest simply upon the saying of the witnesses, nor upon their deposition as it is found written, but to make them come in person, to hear them, to see and contemplate their gestures and countenances, to interrogate them, to make them render a reason for the whole exactly: for I believe that, in so doing, the way would be cut off to many malignities, calumnies and conspiracies of witnesses, who would not be so easy and prone to depose falsely, for the reverence, honour and majesty of a sovereign court before which they would have to answer. And this is what the Emperor Hadrian wrote to Junius Rufinus, proconsul of Macedonia: that he wished to believe witnesses, and not their testimony or depositions; for the faith and authority of witnesses who are present is other, and greater beyond comparison, than that of depositions which are only read and recited <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>, and most often written and dictated more at the appetite of some bad fellow of a commissioner, or of some scribbler of a clerk, than according to the intention and will of the witness. And Callistratus the Jurisconsult, pursuing Hadrian's argument on this matter, says that, upon the accusation which Alexander made against one called Aper of I know not what crimes, forasmuch as Alexander did not produce witnesses, but wished to use only their depositions, Hadrian answered that the testimonies had no place with him, and that he would give them no credit: "for I wish myself," said he, "to interrogate the witnesses" <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. And this is, in my opinion, what our Justinian has left written,

notes.citation: Coras, Annotation XXVI (cross-reference; annot-026, on witnesses who depose on credit)
Digest 22.5.3 (De testibus, l. Testium fides, Callistratus), § Idem divus (D. 22.5.3.3–4 in the modern division)
notes.original: l. iij. P. idem diuus D. de teſtib.
notes.gloss: § 3: Idem divus Hadrianus Iunio Rufino proconsuli Macedoniae rescripsit testibus se, non testimoniis crediturum; § 4, the rescript to Gabinius Maximus: Alia est auctoritas praesentium testium, alia testimoniorum quae recitari solent — "the authority of witnesses who are present is one thing, that of testimonies which are usually read out another", which Coras paraphrases. The P. is the print's sort for the paragraph sign §.

notes.citation: Digest 22.5.3.3, the same paragraph Idem divus, further on (add. = adde, "add", i.e. the continuation of the paragraph just cited)
notes.gloss: Hadrian's letter: Quod crimina obiecerit apud me Alexander Apro et quia non probabat nec testes producebat, sed testimoniis uti volebat, quibus apud me locus non est (nam ipsos interrogare soleo)… — "since he did not prove them nor produce witnesses, but wished to use testimonies, which have no place with me (for I am accustomed to question the witnesses themselves)".

lines: auant auoyent ſi fermement ſouſtenu
le priſonnier eſtre Martin Guerre.
Aduiſent ici les iuges combien il eſt dangereux, &
plein de peril, ſingulierement és matieres criminelles,
où ſe traitte de l'honneur & de la vie de l'homme: d'aſ-
ſeoir iugement ſur la depoſition des teſmoins: leſquels
ſouuentesfois aſſeurent pertinacement choſes fauſſes
pour veritables {a}, dont apres ſont contraints ſe depar-
tir. Voyent auſſi les iuges combien il eſt plus aſſeuré,
meſmes à vn iugement ſouuerain ne ſ'arreſter point
ſimplement au dire des teſmoins, ni à leur depoſition
qu'on trouue eſcrite: mais de les faire venir en perſon-
ne, les ouyr, voir & contempler leurs geſtes & conte-
nances, les interroguer, leur faire rendre raiſon du tout
exactement: car ie cuide qu'ainſi faiſant, ſeroit retren-
ché le chemin à beaucoup de malignitez, calomnies &
conſpirations des teſmoins, qui ne ſe rendroyent ſi fa-
ciles & procliues à fauſſement depoſer, pour la reue-
rence, honneur & majeſté d'vne court ſouueraine, de-
uant laquelle conuiendroit reſpondre: & c'eſt ce que
l'Empereur Adrian eſcriuit à Iune Ruffin, proconſul de
Macedoine, Qu'il vouloit croire aux teſmoins; & non
point à leur teſmoignage ni depoſitions: car la foy &
l'authorité des teſmoios qui ſont preſens eſt autre, &
plus grande ſans comparaiſon, que des depoſitions qui
ſon ſeulement leuës, & recitées {b}: & le plus ſouuent eſ
crites, & dictées, plus à l'appetit d'vn mauuais garçon
de commiſſaire, ou d'vn brouillaçon de greffier, que ſe-
lon l'intention & volonté du teſmoin. Et Calliſtrat Iu-
riſconſulte, pourſuyuant l'argumẽt d'Adrian à ces pro-
pos dit, que ſur l'accuſation que faiſoit Alexandre con-
tre vn appellé Aper, de ie ne ſçay quels crimes, pour-
tant qu'Alexandre ne produiſoit point teſmoins, mais
vouloit vſer ſeulement de leurs depſitions: Adrian re-
ſpondit, que les teſmoignages n'auoyẽt point lieu en-
uers luy, & qu'il n'y donneroit point de foy car ie veux
moy-meſmes, dit-il, interroguer les teſmoings {c}. Et
c'eſt à mon aduis, ce que noſtre Iuſtinien a laiſſé eſcrit,
